scope: How a delivery team's project records (risks, decisions, dependencies, issues, milestones, tasks) reference each other and the findings that raised them: which record carries each link, which links are two-way, how a link names its target so it stays valid when the target moves or closes, and how links are checked for dangling targets. Record-specific fields (decision supersession, issue resolution, blocked milestones, task blockers, risk and dependency fields) stay with their host topics; this research covers the shared linking convention. Safety-critical requirements traceability is context only.
research_type: How-to / troubleshooting (Product / how-to LOW-MEDIUM bar, no escalation); no metric claims were found, so the Statistical bar was not invoked.

questions.text: Best practices: what is current best practice for this topic?
Known solutions: what solutions, patterns, libraries and tools already exist, and how do they compare?
Platform guidelines: what do the platform owners' own guidelines say, for each platform the topic touches (Apple, Android, Windows, web, the databases and runtimes concerned)?
The expert's view: if we hired an expert consultant in this topic, what would they tell us: what to do, what to avoid, and what people usually get wrong?

methodology.method: guidelines/researching/process/research-methodology-and-sources: orient and classify (how-to; traceability between project records), go to the authoritative sources (method owners and standards bodies, the issue trackers' own documentation, the canonical ADR texts, traceability tools' documentation), chain citations, corroborate across independent publishers, record provenance at generation time. Scored per guidelines/researching/evidence/verification-and-trust-scoring.
methodology.search_strategy: WebSearch for each tracker's linking, relation, dependency, sub-issue, milestone, move/transfer and delete documentation (GitHub, Jira, Linear, GitLab); PRINCE2 register composition (public summaries, the manual being paywalled); PMI risk/issue logs; ADR numbering and supersession (Nygard, MADR, adr-tools, Microsoft Learn, Henderson); bidirectional traceability and dangling-link validation (Doorstop, Sphinx-Needs, IBM ELM, Wikipedia, NASA SWEHB); W3C on persistent identifiers; practitioner RAID-log guidance. Every cited page was fetched; quotes were checked against the fetched page text.
methodology.inclusion: Primary: tracker vendors' own documentation of their own features, W3C, Microsoft Learn, the Scrum Guide, the canonical ADR texts and tool sources. Secondary only where no primary source was reachable (PRINCE2 summaries by accredited trainers, Wikipedia for the Gotel and Finkelstein definition, a practitioner course page), and said so in the claim's trust basis.
methodology.exclusion: Vendor marketing pages that do not document a feature; community forum answers; projectteam's own paths, formats and specialist names; safety-standard (DO-178C, ISO 26262) text beyond link direction and dangling-link checking; pages that could not be fetched (PMI library, NASA SWEHB, ISO OBP, the UCL Gotel and Finkelstein PDF).

summary: The topic has no rules of its own, so every verdict is new. The sources converge on a small linking convention. Every record gets a unique identifier that is never reused and carries no status or location, so it stays valid when the record moves or closes (PRINCE2 summaries, Nygard, MADR, W3C; Jira and GitHub redirect moved records' old keys and URLs). A link names its target by that identifier. A two-way relationship is recorded once, as a typed link with a phrase for each direction, and is shown on both records (Jira's outward/inward descriptions, GitLab's bi-directional linked items, GitHub's backlinks and blocked-by/blocking API, Linear's Blocked by/Blocks, adr-tools' reverse link). Records are closed or superseded, never deleted: a deleted GitHub issue's URL becomes page-not-found, while Linear keeps a resolved blocker's relation as Related; a changed decision is a new record that supersedes the old and both are linked (Microsoft Learn, Nygard, adr-tools). Blocked work names its blocker explicitly (GitHub's own guidance). Traceability tools check links: Doorstop errors on a link to an unknown UID and warns on links to inactive items, unlinked items and cycles; Sphinx-Needs warns on dead links unless allowed; IBM ELM marks links suspect when either end changes. The method owners (Scrum Guide, PRINCE2 as publicly summarised) leave the link fields to the team beyond unique identifiers and an integrated register. Strengths supported are SHOULD at most: no source requires (MUST) any of these practices for project records.
open_questions: Whether a two-way link is written in both records' files or written once and its reverse computed by the checker; the trackers compute the reverse, file-based records must choose.
What identifier scheme project records use: one prefix per record type (R-1, D-1, I-1) or one global sequence; the sources require only uniqueness and no reuse.
Whether a link to an unknown identifier fails the check (as Doorstop's error does) or only warns (as Sphinx-Needs does by default).
Whether a link whose target is closed or superseded is reported at all, and if so at what level; Linear keeps it as Related, Doorstop warns when a child links to an inactive parent.
Whether every record must be linked to at least one other record (an orphan check), or only the record types whose host topics require a link.
Whether accepted decision records are immutable (Microsoft Learn, Nygard) or may take dated amendments (Henderson's teams found mutability worked better).
Whether a realised risk keeps its record and links forward to the new issue (the 'realised, see I-01' convention) or is moved to the issue register as PRINCE2 summaries describe.
limitations: PMI's PMBOK Guide and its practice standards, ISO 21502 and ISO 31000 are paywalled; PMI's public library pages and ISO's OBP preview returned 403 to the fetcher, so no claim rests on them.
AXELOS's PRINCE2 manual is paywalled; PRINCE2 is covered only through two accredited trainers' public summaries (PRINCE2 wiki by EMPII Group, ILX Group's prince2.com).

NASA's Software Engineering Handbook (bidirectional traceability, SWE-052/059) returned 403; Gotel and Finkelstein's 1994 definition of requirements traceability is cited through Wikipedia, which quotes it.
The IBM Engineering Lifecycle Management page was read through WebFetch only; a direct download returned 403, so its quote could not be checked a second way.
The Kanban Guide, SAFe and LeSS were not researched for this topic; the Scrum Guide was read and is silent on links between items.
Linear's documentation does not say whether a relation is stored once or twice; it shows Blocked by on one issue and Blocks on the other.
No study or survey measured how often project-record links dangle or what a linking convention saves; no metric claim is made.
Atlassian's RAID-log article body could not be retrieved; practitioner RAID-log guidance found (Smartsheet, Notion) does not address identifiers or cross-references.
Apple, Android and Windows have no bearing on this topic and were not researched.
license: MIT (this research record); quoted material remains under its sources' terms and is quoted for verification.

claims.question: best-practices
claims.claim: Records in a decision log are numbered sequentially and a number is never reused, so a reference to a number keeps naming the same record.
claims.quote: ADRs will be numbered sequentially and monotonically. Numbers will not be reused. | NNNN is a consecutive number
claims.source_type: canonical practitioner article; open-source template documentation
claims.query: Nygard documenting architecture decisions numbered sequentially; MADR template status superseded filename

trust.basis: The originating ADR text and the most-used ADR template agree independently; stable practice, currency not critical. Stated for decision records; extending it to other project records is an inference.

claims.question: best-practices
claims.claim: An identifier that must stay valid should not encode things that change, such as a record's status: links break because people change names, not because they have to.
claims.quote: Cool URIs don't change. | URIs don't change: people change them. | Documents change status - or there would be no point in producing drafts.
claims.query: W3C cool URIs don't change

trust.basis: W3C note by the web's inventor, long-standing; written for web URIs, applied here by analogy to record identifiers; single publisher.

claims.question: best-practices
claims.claim: A changed decision is recorded as a new record that supersedes the original, the original is marked superseded, and the two are linked to each other rather than the old record being edited.
claims.quote: The ADR serves as an append-only log. Don't go back and edit accepted records. If a decision changes, write a new record that supersedes the original and link the two together. | If a later ADR changes or reverses a decision, it may be marked as "deprecated" or "superseded" with a reference to its replacement.

citations.title: Maintain an architecture decision record (ADR) - Microsoft Azure Well-Architected Framework
citations.author: Microsoft

claims.query: Microsoft Well-Architected architecture decision record append-only supersede; Nygard ADR superseded reference to its replacement

trust.basis: Microsoft's current guidance (2026) and the originating ADR article agree independently; Microsoft states it as an imperative.

claims.question: best-practices
claims.claim: Traceability is defined as following an item's life in both directions, from its origins forward and from later work back.
claims.quote: the ability to describe and follow the life of a requirement in both a forwards and backwards direction
claims.query: requirements traceability definition forwards and backwards direction

trust.basis: Secondary: Wikipedia quoting Gotel and Finkelstein's definition, used because the original paper and NASA's SWEHB returned 403; requirements-domain context applied to project records. Second check 2026-11-24: refuted (quote-found yes, supports-claim partly): The definition is of requirements traceability: following "the life of a requirement" forwards and backwards. The claim widens it to traceability of any item; lowered 55->35.

claims.claim: When a risk materialises it becomes an issue, and the register links the risk to the new issue rather than losing the connection.

trust.basis: Two independent secondary sources (no primary PRINCE2 or PMI text reachable); the second is an unattributed course page, so only the risk-to-issue transition is well grounded, the link convention less so.

claims.question: known-solutions
claims.claim: Across trackers, a two-way relationship is recorded once and shown from both records, each side with its own wording, rather than being written separately on each record.
claims.quote: Linked items create bi-directional relationships between work items | At the same time, "Issue B" has an inward link of type blocks that goes back to "Issue A". | By default, references generate a backlink.
claims.query: GitLab linked items bi-directional; Jira inward outward link; GitHub backlink

trust.basis: Three independent vendors' own documentation show the same pattern; the synthesis (record once, show both ways) is this research's reading of their behaviour. Second check 2026-11-24: refuted (quote-found yes, supports-claim partly): The sources say links are bi-directional, that Jira shows one link as inward on the other issue, and that GitHub "will automatically generate another link". None says a link is "recorded once", and GitHub's backlink is a second link with no wording of its own, so "across trackers… each side with its own wording" goes beyond what they say; lowered 85->65.

claims.question: known-solutions
claims.claim: adr-tools writes both ends of a decision link: superseding marks the old record superseded and links it to the new one, and a plain link writes a reverse link into the existing record.

claims.query: adr-tools adr new supersede link reverse link

claims.question: experts-view
claims.claim: Practitioners report that links assumed to exist are often missing, and the gap is found only when someone needs them.
claims.quote: However, it was soon identified that the fundamental traceability links between requirements and test cases were missing. This lack of traceability impeded the implementation of a solution to help the company deal with its quality issues.

citations.title: When Traceability Goes Awry: an Industrial Experience Report
citations.author: Davide Fucci, Emil Alégroth, Thomas Axelsson

claims.query: when traceability goes awry industrial experience report

trust.basis: One industrial case (an anecdote, not a population result) in a preprint; supports the failure mode, not its frequency. Second check 2026-11-24: refuted (quote-found yes, supports-claim partly): The abstract reports one case, at a single telecom company, where links were missing. It says traceability is "often assumed to exist", not that links are "often missing", and it does not say gaps are found only when someone needs them; lowered 52->32.
